query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing approximately 5 atomic% Cr into the NbMoTaW alloy will promote the in situ formation of fine, ductile secondary phases along grain boundaries, thereby improving room‐temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while preserving the alloy’s high-temperature BCC stability and mechanical strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW, known for excellent high-temperature strength but with poor room-temperature ductility and uncertain experimental irradiation response.
generation.intervention: Add ~5 atomic% chromium during alloy synthesis to create a quinary alloy (NbMoTaW + 5% Cr).
generation.conditions: Room temperature for tensile ductility assessment, high-temperature conditions (up to 1600 °C) for maintaining mechanical performance, and irradiation (e.g., helium ion implantation at reactor-relevant energies/fluences) to assess irradiation tolerance.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ–formed, fine, ductile secondary phase precipitates (Cr-rich) preferentially located along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The Cr addition is expected to result in controlled local compositional fluctuations that nucleate in situ ductile precipitates. These precipitates can act as barriers to crack propagation and effective defect sinks during irradiation, leading to improved dislocation mobility at room temperature and mitigating irradiation-induced phenomena (e.g., He bubble coalescence, amorphization or precipitation) without compromising the high-temperature stability of the BCC matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the Cr-doped alloy should exhibit higher room-temperature ductility (i.e., improved strain-to-failure), maintain high strength at elevated temperatures (up to 1600 °C), and show reduced irradiation-induced damage (e.g., smaller or more uniformly distributed He bubbles, less segregation).
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized, equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW exhibiting high high-temperature strength but poor ductility at room temperature and computationally predicted irradiation behavior.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated within the operating temperature range from room temperature to 1600 °C and under irradiation conditions typical of helium implantation experiments that simulate reactor-relevant displacement damage and He production.
generation.uncertainty: The exact size, volume fraction, and distribution of the Cr-rich precipitates, as well as their long-term thermal and irradiation stability, remain uncertain. Additionally, there is uncertainty regarding whether 5 atomic% Cr is near the optimal doping level to balance the ductility improvement without inducing embrittlement via excessive secondary phase formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: a control group of pure NbMoTaW and an experimental group of NbMoTaW with 5 atomic% Cr added. Subject both groups to identical thermomechanical processing. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) compression/tensile tests. Irradiate matched samples with helium ions at reactor-relevant energies and fluences. Use complementary microstructural characterization (TEM, APT) to evaluate the presence, size, and distribution of secondary phases and irradiation-induced defects.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile ductility (strain-to-failure, yield and ultimate tensile strength)
Irradiation damage metrics (e.g., size and distribution of He bubbles, defect density, evidence of amorphization or precipitation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-doped NbMoTaW does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility or irradiation resistance relative to the control (and/or if detrimental phase formation leads to embrittlement or amplified irradiation damage), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: W-based refractory HEAs (RHEAs) have been recently developed in the context of high-temperature applications, showing high melting temperature (above 2873 K) and superior mechanical strength at high temperatures compared to Ni-based superalloys or pure W,. Combining the two approaches above, the authors have recently developed a refractory low-activation HEA based on W-Ta-Cr-V. Its response to loop formation under ion irradiation and He implantation is enhanced compared to previously developed W-based alloys, showing no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries upon heavy ion irradiation and He implantation, respectively. However, this quaternary RHEA demonstrated Cr- and V-rich precipitates which could be detrimental to mechanical properties in terms of embrittlement. In this study, a design strategy to further improve the overall response of the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA is introduced and resulted in the development of a quinary RHEA with improved resistance to high-temperature and irradiation environments. cited_evidence.text: Using electronic structure calculations as implemented in VASP code, formation, and migration energies of He were computed in the W-Ta-Cr-V system. The He average migration energy was found to be 0.156 eV in the alloy compared to 0.06 to 0.081 eV in pure W and the He formation energy was approximately 2 times lower,. This rough energy landscape implies that He has a higher tendency to quickly find a fairly stable site that can act as a bubble nuclei, and also to bind to other slowly migrating He interstitial atoms. The clustering of He will slow them further down and a trend for smaller and lesser bubble nucleation will follow, and therefore, uniform bubble distribution with no preferential bubble formation at the grain boundaries or a wide distribution of bubble sizes occur. The absence of preferential bubble formation at grain boundaries can also stem from the high migration barrier of He-vacancy complexes, which still needs to be further investigated. Grain boundaries can also play a role in the irradiation resistance of the alloy acting as defect sinks. APT was performed on a sample irradiated at 1050 K to ~8 dpa using 3-MeV Cu+. After irradiation, we observed no compositional layering of any element (Fig. 5, A to H). Although elemental segregation at grain boundaries is still observed, the precipitation of Cr-rich phases in the grain matrices occurred, as shown in the top-down view of an APT reconstruction with a 25 atomic % (at %) Cr isocomposition surface (Fig. 5, M and N). We have also analyzed the compositional partitioning between the precipitate and the grain matrix (Fig. 5O), showing the enrichment of Cr and V and the depletion of W and Ta inside the black spots. These precipitates are of ~3 to 5 nm in size and show a density of ~0.03 nm−2, both of which are consistent with the in situ–irradiated 8-dpa sample (similar size and density). Therefore, we can conclude that the black spots observed in the irradiated HEA samples at high temperature are Cr- and V-rich precipitates and not irradiation-created dislocation loops.

In the present study, we succeeded in tuning the microstructure and improving the room-temperature tensile properties of a high-performance Co-rich Co35Cr25Ni15Mn15Fe10 (at%) TRIP-HEA, achieved by using thermomechanical processings of rolling and heat-treatment. The correlation between the microstructures and the strengthening mechanism of the samples at each stage was clarified. The grains were non-uniformly refined by the hot-rolling process but were significantly refined and homogenized after cold-rolling, followed by appropriate heat treatment. The grain size was refined from 144.4 μm to 1.83 μm by cold-rolling and subsequent annealing at 973 K; meanwhile, the Cr-rich σ-phase with a volume fraction of 0.413% and an average size of 118.8 nm was formed. It was found that grain refinement is the most effective method for enhancing the tensile strength while retaining ductility, whereas the formation of incoherent precipitates slightly improves strength but sacrifices ductility.
